screen: Welcome (the first screen a new user ever sees)
whenSeen: On a fresh install, and any time the user has no saved homes and no half-finished homes — the app skips the saved-homes list and opens straight here. Also reached by tapping "Add a home" on the saved-homes screen.

strings.text: NO SIGN-UP · NO PHONE NUMBER
strings.condition: Always. Written in the code as "No sign-up · No phone number"; the section-label component forces it to capitals on screen.
strings.concern: Fine, but the same promise is repeated almost word for word on the Privacy screen ("There is no account, no sign-up and no phone number") and again in Settings ("No account, no phone number"). Three different wordings of one idea.

strings.text: See your home's Vastu — and exactly what to do about it.
strings.condition: Always — the biggest text on the first screen.
strings.concern: A promise the app does not keep for two of the three people it is speaking to. This headline sits ABOVE the question that asks whether you are buying, building or living somewhere — and only the "building" answer is offered layout changes in the report. A buyer or an existing resident is told "exactly what to do about it" before the app knows it will not be telling them that. "Exactly" is also the strongest word on the screen and is the one that would be read as a guaranteed outcome.

strings.text: Upload or draw your plan. Mark North. See your score and what to do.
strings.condition: Always.
strings.concern: "Mark North" is the app's own internal name for a step; a home buyer reading this does not yet know that marking north is something they will be asked to do, or why. It repeats the headline's "what to do" promise a second time in three lines.

strings.text: WHAT BRINGS YOU HERE?
strings.condition: Always. Written as "What brings you here?"; rendered in capitals.
strings.concern: None.

strings.text: I am buying a home
strings.condition: Always — first of three choice cards.
strings.concern: None.

strings.text: Deciding between options
strings.condition: Always — subtitle of the first choice card.
strings.concern: None.

strings.text: I am building a home
strings.condition: Always — second choice card.
strings.concern: None.

strings.text: The plan is not final yet
strings.condition: Always — subtitle of the second choice card.
strings.concern: None.

strings.text: I already live here
strings.condition: Always — third choice card.
strings.concern: None.

strings.text: Looking for remedies
strings.condition: Always — subtitle of the third choice card.
strings.concern: "Remedies" is the only place on this screen the word appears, and it quietly tells the reader that this answer gets a different kind of report from the other two. It is also the one word here that could be read as a health or fortune promise.

strings.condition: Appears inside a small circle on whichever of the three cards has been tapped.
strings.concern: The tick is a bare character with no spoken label, and the card itself is not marked as "selected" for a screen reader — it is only marked as a button. Someone using a screen reader cannot tell which of the three answers they have chosen, and cannot tell why Continue is refusing to work.

strings.text: Continue
strings.condition: Always visible. Greyed out and unresponsive until one of the three cards has been tapped.
strings.concern: The button is dead on arrival with nothing on screen saying why. A reader who taps it and gets no response has no sentence to read.

strings.text: Privacy
strings.condition: Always — a quiet text link under Continue. This is the only way a brand-new user can reach the privacy policy, because the gear that leads to Settings only exists on the saved-homes screen.
strings.concern: Ambiguous about what a tap will do: it reads like a settings heading rather than "read our privacy policy", and it sits directly under the main button where a stray tap is likely.

screen: Your plans (the saved-homes list)
whenSeen: On opening the app when at least one home is saved, half-finished, or could not be read. Also returned to after Back from Settings.

strings.text: Your plans
strings.condition: Always.
strings.concern: The screen calls the items "plans" in its title, "homes" in the button below it ("Add a home"), "floor plan" in its empty state, and "homes" again in every dialog. Four names for one thing on one screen.

strings.text: Settings
strings.condition: Always — the spoken label of the gear button in the top right. Sighted users see only the character ⚙.
strings.concern: None.

strings.text: 1 home can't be opened
strings.condition: When exactly one saved home cannot be read by this version of the app.
strings.concern: None.

strings.text: 2 homes can't be opened
strings.condition: When two or more saved homes cannot be read. The number is the real count — "3 homes can't be opened", and so on.
strings.concern: None.

strings.text: It's still on your phone — nothing has been deleted. An app update may open it again.
strings.condition: Assembled sentence, shown when exactly one home cannot be read.
strings.concern: "An app update may open it again" is a promise nobody can keep — no update is planned or guaranteed, and this sits directly above a Remove button whose own warning says an update will NOT be able to bring it back. The two sentences pull in opposite directions on the same card.

strings.text: They're still on your phone — nothing has been deleted. An app update may open them again.
strings.condition: Assembled sentence, shown when two or more homes cannot be read.
strings.concern: Same as above.

strings.text: Home 2 · 3 days ago
strings.condition: One line per unreadable home, inside that card. The first part is the home's own name (auto-named "Home 1", "Home 2"… unless renamed); the second is the date wording listed under "Date wording" below.
strings.concern: None.

strings.text: Remove Home 2
strings.condition: Spoken label of the ✕ next to each unreadable home. The name is the real home name.
strings.concern: None.

strings.text: Remove
strings.condition: Printed next to the ✕ on each unreadable home's line.
strings.concern: It looks exactly like a button and is not one — it is plain text, and the tappable thing is the small ✕ beside it. Tapping the word "Remove" does nothing at all. This is the clearest "ambiguous about what a tap will do" case in the whole set.

strings.text: No plans yet
strings.condition: Only when there are no finished homes AND no half-finished ones AND no unreadable ones. In practice a first-time user never sees it, because the app opens on Welcome instead; it appears after deleting everything from Settings.
strings.concern: None.

strings.text: Add your first floor plan to see its Vastu score.
strings.condition: Same as above.
strings.concern: Says "floor plan" where the button underneath says "home" and the title says "plans".

strings.text: We changed a rule — your score is unchanged
strings.condition: On the notice card at the top of the list, when the Vastu rules have been updated since these homes were scored and not one home's number moved.
strings.concern: None.

strings.text: Your score has changed
strings.condition: On the notice card, when there is exactly one affected home and its number did move.
strings.concern: Unlike the other two variants it does not say WHY on the heading line, and it reads as though the home changed rather than the rules. The reason is further down the card.

strings.text: We changed a rule — some scores moved
strings.condition: On the notice card, in every other case (several homes, some moved).
strings.concern: None.

strings.condition: One line per affected home on the notice card, when that home's number moved. The numbers are the old and new scores out of ten.
strings.concern: None.

strings.text: Home 1: 7.1 — unchanged
strings.condition: One line per affected home on the notice card, when that home's number did not move.
strings.concern: None.

strings.text: Your score has not moved, and nothing has been taken out of your report. We corrected two lines in it. Three of the things we say we could not check pointed you at a screen the app no longer has; they now point at the button on your report that actually asks. The fourth — a mirror facing a bed, or a beam running over one — used to promise we would check it if you answered a few more questions, and there has never been a question for it. It now says plainly that we do not check that one, and why.
strings.condition: The explanation paragraph on the notice card. It is not written in the screen's code — it comes from the rule data, so it changes with every rule release. This is exactly what it says today.
strings.concern: Far longer than it needs to be, and written in the team's voice, not the reader's — "we corrected two lines in it", "pointed you at a screen the app no longer has" is release-note language about our own past mistakes, on the first card an older reader meets in daylight. At large font it fills the whole screen.

strings.text: Got it
strings.condition: On the score-change notice card. Tapping it accepts the new numbers and the card never returns.
strings.concern: Does not say that the new numbers are being saved over the old ones. "Got it" reads as "dismiss", not "accept".

strings.text: STILL TO FINISH
strings.condition: Above the half-finished homes, when there is at least one. Written as "Still to finish".
strings.concern: None.

strings.text: FINISHED
strings.condition: Above the completed homes, but only when there is also at least one half-finished home. Written as "Finished".
strings.concern: None.

strings.text: Unfinished home
strings.condition: The title of a half-finished home's row when the user never gave it a name.
strings.concern: Identical text on every unnamed unfinished home, so two of them are indistinguishable — the very problem the rename box exists to prevent.

strings.text: 5 rooms so far · yesterday
strings.condition: Subtitle of a half-finished home. "5" is the real count of rooms placed; the date wording is listed under "Date wording" below.
strings.concern: None.

strings.text: 1 room so far · today
strings.condition: Same line when exactly one room has been placed.
strings.concern: None.

strings.text: carry on with this home
strings.condition: What a screen reader announces the tap will do on a half-finished home's row.
strings.concern: None.

strings.text: Throw away this unfinished home
strings.condition: Spoken label of the ✕ at the right of a half-finished home's row.
strings.concern: None.

strings.text: Carry on
strings.condition: Printed at the right of every half-finished home's row, after the ✕.
strings.concern: Looks like a button, is plain text. It happens to work because the whole row is tappable — but it sits immediately to the RIGHT of the ✕ that throws the home away, so the word and the destructive control read as one control. A shaky tap aimed at "Carry on" lands on delete.

strings.text: Buying · today
strings.condition: Subtitle of a finished home. The first word comes from the answer given on the Welcome screen — the three possible values are "Buying", "Building" and "Living".
strings.concern: "Living" on its own is not a sentence and not what the user chose — they chose "I already live here". The word is machine-generated from an internal code rather than written, which is why it reads oddly.

strings.text: Rename Home 1
strings.condition: Spoken label of the pencil at the right of a finished home's row. The name is the real home name.
strings.concern: None.

strings.condition: The score at the right of every finished home's row, always with one decimal (so 5 shows as "5.0"). On a phone set to a comma-decimal language it reads "4,7".
strings.concern: None.

strings.condition: Printed under the score on every finished home's row.
strings.concern: A screen reader reads the whole row as one sentence and announces this as a stray slash — "Home 1, Buying, today, four point seven, slash ten". The app already has a properly spoken version of the score ("Score 4.7 out of 10") and it is not used here.

strings.text: Add a home
strings.condition: Always, at the bottom of the screen.
strings.concern: None.

strings.text: Rename this home
strings.condition: After tapping the pencil on a finished home.
strings.concern: None.

strings.text: Home name
strings.condition: The field label in the rename box.
strings.concern: None.

strings.text: e.g. Dwarka flat
strings.condition: Greyed text inside the rename field, shown only while the field is empty.
strings.concern: None.

strings.text: You already have a home called this. Please pick a different name.
strings.condition: Appears live, as the user types, when the typed name matches any other home on the screen — including a half-finished one or one that cannot be opened. Save is greyed out while it shows.
strings.concern: None.

strings.text: Cancel
strings.condition: In the rename box.
strings.concern: Every other dialog in the app uses a plain-English cancel ("Keep it", "Keep my data"). This one uses "Cancel". Inconsistent.

strings.text: Save
strings.condition: In the rename box. Greyed out while the field is empty or the name is already taken.
strings.concern: None.

strings.text: Throw away this unfinished home?
strings.condition: After tapping the ✕ on a half-finished home.
strings.concern: None.

strings.text: The 5 rooms you placed will be gone, and we can't bring them back. Your finished homes aren't affected.
strings.condition: Assembled sentence in that dialog. "5" is the real count.
strings.concern: None.

strings.text: The 1 room you placed will be gone, and we can't bring them back. Your finished homes aren't affected.
strings.condition: The same sentence when exactly one room was placed.
strings.concern: Broken grammar in the one-room case: "The 1 room… we can't bring them back". Should read "The one room you placed will be gone, and we can't bring it back."

strings.text: Keep it
strings.condition: The safe choice in the throw-away dialog.
strings.concern: None.

strings.text: Throw it away
strings.condition: The destructive choice in the throw-away dialog. Cannot be undone.
strings.concern: The destructive button is styled as the quieter, outlined one and the safe button as the solid one — so the visually louder button is the one that does nothing. Same pattern in the other two destructive dialogs.

strings.text: Remove Home 2 for good?
strings.condition: After tapping the ✕ next to a home that cannot be opened. The name is the real home name.
strings.concern: None.

strings.text: This home can't be opened, so we can't show you what's in it. Removing it deletes it from your phone — a future app update won't be able to bring it back. Your other homes aren't affected.
strings.condition: In that dialog.
strings.concern: Directly contradicts the card the user tapped from, which said "An app update may open it again."

strings.text: Keep it
strings.condition: The safe choice in the remove dialog.
strings.concern: None.

strings.text: Remove it
strings.condition: The destructive choice in the remove dialog.
strings.concern: See the styling note above — the destructive button is the quieter-looking one.

screen: Add your home (choosing how to enter a plan)
whenSeen: Immediately after tapping Continue on the Welcome screen, and after tapping "Add a home" on the saved-homes list (which walks through Welcome first).

strings.text: Add your home
strings.condition: Always.
strings.concern: None.

strings.text: Place your rooms on a simple grid — or try a sample to see the whole flow first.
strings.condition: Always — the sentence directly under the heading.
strings.concern: Describes only two of the three choices, and skips the one listed FIRST. A reader is told about the grid and the sample, then handed "Upload a plan" at the top of the list with no mention of it in the intro.

strings.text: Upload a plan
strings.condition: Always — first of three cards. Tapping it goes to the consent explanation the first time, and straight to the camera/file picker afterwards.
strings.concern: The card gives no hint that the first tap leads to a permission/consent screen rather than to the camera.

strings.text: Photo or PDF · we read it, you check every room
strings.condition: Subtitle of the first card.
strings.concern: None.

strings.text: Draw it on a grid
strings.condition: Always — second card.
strings.concern: None.

strings.text: Place room blocks by hand · stays on your phone
strings.condition: Subtitle of the second card.
strings.concern: "Stays on your phone" is only said on this card, which by contrast implies the upload card does not — true, but the reader is left to infer the most important privacy fact on the screen from an absence.

strings.text: Try a sample plan
strings.condition: Always — third card.
strings.concern: None.

strings.text: See the whole flow in ten seconds
strings.condition: Subtitle of the third card.
strings.concern: A specific time promise the app has no way to keep — the sample still walks the user through marking north and reaching a report.

strings.text: You confirm every room yourself — nothing is scored until you say it's right.
strings.condition: Always — the grey note at the bottom of the screen.
strings.concern: None.

strings.text: SOON
strings.condition: Never, in the shipped app. The pill exists in the code and no card is set to use it, so this is copy that can no longer appear.
strings.concern: Dead copy. Harmless on screen, but it is the leftover of a "coming soon" pattern that the project has ruled out, and the file's own description still says upload is shown as "coming soon", which is no longer true.

strings.condition: The three symbols in the coloured tiles on the three cards.
strings.concern: None of the three has a spoken label, so a screen reader either says nothing or reads a meaningless symbol before the card title.

screen: Settings
whenSeen: After tapping the gear in the top right of the saved-homes list. Not reachable at all until the user has at least one saved, unfinished or unreadable home.

strings.text: Back
strings.condition: Spoken label of the ‹ chevron at the top left. Sighted users see only the chevron.
strings.concern: None.

strings.text: Settings
strings.condition: Always.
strings.concern: None.

strings.text: PREFERENCES
strings.condition: Always. Written as "Preferences"; rendered in capitals.
strings.concern: There is exactly one row under it and it cannot be tapped or changed, so the heading promises a section of choices that does not exist.

strings.text: Vastu reading
strings.condition: Always — the only row under Preferences.
strings.concern: Means nothing on its own. It is not a preference, cannot be tapped, and does not say what it is telling you.

strings.text: 8 directions + centre
strings.condition: The value shown at the right of the "Vastu reading" row. Fixed — it never changes.
strings.concern: A fact with no question attached. The reader is shown a value in a settings list, cannot change it, and is not told what it affects.

strings.text: WHICH AI READS A PLAN · TESTING
strings.condition: Only on a build that has a working plan-reading key. On a build without one, this heading, the buttons under it and the paragraph under those are all hidden completely. Written as "Which AI reads a plan · testing".
strings.concern: Straight developer language on a screen a paying customer opens. The word "testing" tells a buyer this part of the product is unfinished, and nothing explains what it means for them.

strings.text: Auto
strings.condition: First of the choice buttons in that section. Selected by default.
strings.concern: None on its own — but see the model names below.

strings.text: GPT 5.6 Luna
strings.condition: A choice button in that section. The name is derived from the reading service's own product code, currently "openai/gpt-5.6-luna".
strings.concern: A product name from another company, meaningless to an Indian home buyer, shown as a choice they are invited to make with nothing telling them which is better or what changes.

strings.text: Gemini 3.1 Pro
strings.condition: A choice button in that section, from the code "google/gemini-3.1-pro-preview".
strings.concern: Same as above.

strings.text: Auto is the normal choice — it asks GPT 5.6 Luna and gets a second opinion when needed. A named pick reads with that one only, and now stays chosen if you try a plan again.
strings.condition: Assembled sentence under those buttons. The model name in the middle is filled in from the app's reader settings.
strings.concern: "and now stays chosen" is release-note language — "now" only means something to someone who used an earlier version. "Gets a second opinion" also quietly tells the reader the plan may be sent to a second outside service, which the privacy screen does not mention.

strings.text: DATA & PRIVACY
strings.condition: Always. Written as "Data & privacy".
strings.concern: None.

strings.text: Your plans stay on this device
strings.condition: Always — first row of the data section. Cannot be tapped.
strings.concern: None.

strings.text: On
strings.condition: The green value at the right of that row. Never changes.
strings.concern: "On" makes an unchangeable fact look like a switch the user could turn off. It sits directly above a row that DOES flip when tapped and looks identical.

strings.text: Reading uploaded plans online
strings.condition: Always — second row of the data section. Tapping the row flips the setting immediately, with no confirmation.
strings.concern: Nothing on the row says a tap will change it, and it looks the same as the row above it that does nothing. Turning it off silently changes what happens next time the user uploads a plan, and there is no undo prompt.

strings.text: Allowed
strings.condition: The value at the right of that row once the user has agreed to online plan reading.
strings.concern: The consent screen, the privacy screen and this row use three different words for the same state. Here it is "Allowed"; the privacy text calls it "choose to have a floor plan read for you".

strings.text: Off
strings.condition: The value at the right of that row when the user has never agreed, or has switched it back off.
strings.concern: None.

strings.text: Privacy
strings.condition: Always — opens the privacy policy inside the app.
strings.concern: None.

strings.text: Honesty & sources
strings.condition: Always — opens the page explaining how each Vastu rule is tagged.
strings.concern: Gives no clue what is behind it. A reader looking for the disclaimer, or for where the rules come from, has no reason to guess this row.

strings.text: Delete all my data
strings.condition: Always — shown in red. Opens a confirmation box.
strings.concern: None.

strings.condition: Shown at the right of the Privacy, Honesty & sources and Delete all my data rows.
strings.concern: A bare character with no spoken label. On the Delete row it is red and sits where the other rows show a value, so it reads as a value rather than "opens something".

strings.text: No account, no phone number. Only a plan you upload ever leaves your phone.
strings.condition: Always — the grey line under the data section.
strings.concern: Not true on this very screen. When the app has recorded a crash, the section immediately below offers to email a crash report — which also leaves the phone. The sentence says "only", and the button underneath breaks it.

strings.text: SOMETHING WENT WRONG
strings.condition: Only when the app crashed the last time it was used. Written as "Something went wrong".
strings.concern: None.

strings.text: The app crashed last time. Emailing us what happened helps us fix it. You read it first, and it says nothing about you or your homes.
strings.condition: Same condition — only after a crash.
strings.concern: None.

strings.text: Send what went wrong
strings.condition: Only after a crash. Opens the phone's email app with the report already written.
strings.concern: On a phone with no email app set up, tapping this does nothing at all and says nothing — no message, no error, the card just stays. The reader is left tapping a button that appears broken.

strings.text: No thanks
strings.condition: Only after a crash. Deletes the report and the section never comes back for that crash.
strings.concern: Does not say the report is thrown away for good. "No thanks" reads as "not now".

strings.text: VastuFirst — something went wrong
strings.condition: The subject line of the crash email, already filled in when the user's email app opens.
strings.concern: None.

strings.text: Anything you were doing when it happened (optional):
strings.condition: The first line of the crash email body, above two blank lines and then the technical detail.
strings.concern: None.

strings.text: --- technical detail, nothing personal ---
strings.condition: The separator line in the crash email, above the technical text.
strings.concern: None.

strings.text: Delete all your data?
strings.condition: After tapping "Delete all my data".
strings.concern: The row says "my data" and the box says "your data" — one of them is written from the user's side, the other from ours.

strings.text: This permanently removes every saved home from this device, and any plan you photographed. It can't be undone.
strings.condition: In that confirmation box.
strings.concern: The privacy screen describes the same button and does NOT mention the photographs. Two screens, two different promises about what the same button deletes.

strings.text: Keep my data
strings.condition: The safe choice in the delete box.
strings.concern: The two other destructive boxes in the app say "Keep it". Three dialogs, two different cancel words.

strings.text: Delete everything
strings.condition: The destructive choice. Wipes every saved home, every half-finished home and every photographed plan, with no undo.
strings.concern: Styled as the quieter, outlined button while the safe choice is the solid one — the loudest button on the most dangerous box is the one that does nothing.

screen: Honesty & sources
whenSeen: After tapping "Honesty & sources" in Settings. Not reachable any other way, so a user who has not yet saved a home can never see the disclaimer.

strings.text: Back
strings.condition: Spoken label of the ‹ chevron.
strings.concern: None.

strings.text: Honesty & sources
strings.condition: Always.
strings.concern: None.

strings.text: Vastu is a traditional practice. This is guidance for your own decisions — not a guaranteed outcome.
strings.condition: Always — the boxed disclaimer at the top.
strings.concern: This is the legal safety net, and it lives behind a gear icon that only appears once a home has been saved — so a first-time reader can buy into the Welcome screen's "exactly what to do about it" without ever seeing this sentence.

strings.text: HOW WE TAG EVERY RULE
strings.condition: Always. Written as "How we tag every rule".
strings.concern: None.

strings.text: From classical text
strings.condition: Always — the first coloured tag.
strings.concern: None.

strings.text: Traceable to a named source, with citation.
strings.condition: Always — under the first tag.
strings.concern: "With citation" is bookish; and the screen never shows the reader where to see one.

strings.text: Traditional practice
strings.condition: Always — the second coloured tag.
strings.concern: The exact phrase "traditional practice" is also used four lines above in "Vastu is a traditional practice", where it means something completely different. One page, one phrase, two meanings.

strings.text: Reasoned from the mandala; widely taught.
strings.condition: Always — under the second tag.
strings.concern: "Mandala" is used with no explanation here, on the one screen whose whole job is to explain where rules come from. The word belongs in the product; a half-line saying what it is would not cost the vocabulary anything.

strings.text: Modern practice
strings.condition: Always — the third coloured tag.
strings.concern: None.

strings.text: 20th-century. Honesty about age, not a warning.
strings.condition: Always — under the third tag.
strings.concern: Reads like a note the team wrote to itself. The second half answers a question the reader has not asked yet, and the first half is a fragment rather than a sentence.

strings.text: Schools disagree
strings.condition: Always — the fourth coloured tag.
strings.concern: None.

strings.text: Two readings shown, neither chosen for you.
strings.condition: Always — under the fourth tag.
strings.concern: None.

strings.text: We never use fear, urgency, or promises of wealth, health or fortune. Where the tradition contradicts itself, we show you both sides.
strings.condition: Always — the closing paragraph.
strings.concern: This is the product's stated position and it is contradicted by the first thing a new user reads: the Welcome screen promises "exactly what to do about it", which is an outcome promise. This page is also where that clash is most visible if anyone ever compares the two.

screen: Privacy (the policy, inside the app)
whenSeen: Two ways in: the quiet "Privacy" link under Continue on the very first screen, and the "Privacy" row in Settings.

strings.text: Back
strings.condition: Spoken label of the ‹ chevron.
strings.concern: None.

strings.text: Privacy
strings.condition: Always.
strings.concern: None.

strings.text: Your homes never leave your phone.
strings.condition: Always — the boldest line on the page, in a green-accented card at the top.
strings.concern: The strongest claim on the page, and the page's own third section is titled "The one thing that leaves your phone" and explains that an uploaded floor plan is sent to an outside AI service. A reader who stops at the headline — which is what a headline is for — is left with the wrong understanding of the one thing that matters here.

strings.text: Everything you draw, every score and every report is worked out on this device and saved only on this device. There is no account, no sign-up and no phone number.
strings.condition: Always — under that headline.
strings.concern: "Everything you draw" is doing quiet work: it is true of drawn homes and silent about uploaded ones. The exception is three sections further down.

strings.text: WHAT WE COLLECT
strings.condition: Always. Written as "What we collect".
strings.concern: None.

strings.text: Nothing about you. We do not ask for your name, email, phone number or location, and the app has no account to sign in to. The homes you draw, their scores and their reports are stored only in the app's own private storage on your phone, where no other app can read them.
strings.condition: Always.
strings.concern: None.

strings.text: THE ONE THING THAT LEAVES YOUR PHONE
strings.condition: Always. Written as "The one thing that leaves your phone".
strings.concern: None.

strings.text: If you choose to have a floor plan read for you, that one picture is sent to an AI service to be turned into rooms, and the rooms come back. The app asks you before it does this, every first time, and you can turn it off again in Settings. The picture is not stored by us and is not linked to you — there is nothing to link it to. Drawing your home by hand needs no internet at all and gives the same score.

screen: Before we start — consent to send your plan
whenSeen: The gate immediately before the upload screen. Shown the first time the user chooses to have a plan read, and again any time the permission has been switched off in Settings or the consent version was bumped. Nothing can reach the internet until this screen is answered.

strings.text: Before we start
Your plan leaves this phone
Everything else happens on your phone. Reading a plan does not — so here is exactly what happens.
What we send
The one picture or PDF you choose. Nothing else — no name, no phone number, no location.
Who reads it
A relay called OpenRouter passes it to an AI model from OpenAI — and sometimes a second one from Google for a second opinion. Their computers are abroad.
strings.concern: Two problems. (1) "A relay called OpenRouter" is company jargon for a reader who will not know what a relay is, and naming three foreign companies on a consent screen is the sentence most likely to make an older buyer back out. (2) It can be untrue: Settings lets the user pin one named reader, and if they pin the Google one the plan goes ONLY to Google — never to OpenAI, never as "a second opinion". The consent text does not change to match, so the person has agreed to something different from what happens.

strings.text: What we ask it
Only to read what is printed on your plan — the room names and sizes, and where each room sits. It is never asked anything about Vastu.
strings.concern: "and where each room sits" sets up an expectation the very next screen contradicts: on most real plans the result screen says "we can't trust where each one sits — and we don't guess". The consent says we ask for placement; the app then quietly throws it away. Truthful in isolation, misleading read alongside the screen after it.

strings.text: What we keep
Nothing. Your plan is not stored by us, and it stays in your phone's own storage.
strings.concern: "Nothing" overstates it. When the plan is photographed inside the app, the picture is written to the app's own storage and stays there until the next scan or until the user runs "Delete all my data". A reader hears "we keep nothing" and would not expect a picture of their home still sitting on the phone.

strings.text: Who works out your score
Your phone does, on its own, exactly as it does for a home you draw by hand.
You can turn this off again at any time in Settings.
I agree — read my plan
Rather not?
Draw your home on the grid instead. It takes a few minutes, nothing leaves your phone, and the score is exactly the same.
strings.concern: "the score is exactly the same" is a promise the app cannot keep. Drawing by hand and reading a plan produce different room shapes and sizes, and the score is computed from those shapes. The same home done both ways can score differently. screen: Report — the words of each problem (from the rule data)
whenSeen: Whatever problems this home has. The headline is always visible; the explanation is behind the price for every room except the entrance, kitchen and toilets.

strings.text: Toilet in the North-East

A toilet stands in the North-East, the corner the tradition guards most closely. This is Ishanya — Shiva's quarter, the water element; in the mandala grid, the head of the Purusha. Every school examined calls waste here the single most serious placement. A toilet belongs in the North-West — Vayu's quarter, whose moving air carries waste out.
strings.concern: "the head of the Purusha" — the term is used as though known. It recurs in four more explanations and is never once defined.

strings.text: Kitchen in the North-East

The kitchen's fire stands in the North-East, Ishanya, the water quarter. A kitchen belongs in the South-East — Agneya, Agni's quarter, fire's own element. Fire set against water opposes the zone's element, so every school warns against this.
Staircase or heavy weight in the centre

A staircase or heavy weight stands on the centre, which the texts say must stay open. The centre is the Brahmasthan — Brahma's own square, the element of space. The Manasara text says outright it must stay open and unweighted — a direct textual violation, not a matter of interpretation. That is why tradition keeps a courtyard at a home's middle.
strings.concern: "a direct textual violation" is the app's own voice slipping into legal-sounding language. Everything around it is written for a home buyer.

strings.text: Cut or missing North-East corner

The plan is missing part of its North-East corner, the ground the tradition values most. That corner is Ishanya — the head of the mandala grid, its most auspicious square. The same tradition welcomes a North-East extension, yet calls a cut there a serious defect.
South-West extension

The plan pushes out at the South-West, the corner meant to stay square and still. That corner is Nairritya — earth's element, the feet of the Purusha. The tradition wants it heaviest and most settled — the firm corner the home rests against. Pushing it outward unbalances exactly that.
Main entrance on the South-West corner
strings.concern: Says "Main entrance" where every other screen in the app says "front door". The editor was deliberately changed to say front door for exactly this reason; the rule data was not.

strings.text: The main entrance stands on the South-West corner — the one door placement every school examined prohibits. The 32-position door table names these positions Yama and Gandharva; in the mandala grid this is the heaviest, most closed corner, meant to stay solid. The entrance is the reading's highest-weighted element, so its position outweighs any single room.
Master bedroom in the North-East or South-East

The master bedroom sits in a light corner — the North-East or South-East — not the heavy South-West. The head of the household should rest in the South-West: Nairritya, earth's element, the most settled quarter. The North-East is the lightest square, kept open rather than slept in; the South-East is Agneya, Agni's fire quarter — no place for rest.
Toilet in the South-West

A toilet stands in the South-West, the corner that anchors the whole home. The South-West is Nairritya — earth's element, meant to stay heavy and undisturbed. The toilet is the one room the tradition holds impure, where things leave the house. Setting it on the anchoring corner works directly against that.
Water stored against the mandala
strings.concern: "against the mandala" as a headline assumes the reader knows what a mandala is and that the home is laid on one. It is the only headline in the set built on a term rather than a room and a direction.

strings.text: The water is stored the wrong way round — weight in the light corner, or water under the heavy one. The mandala grid draws water to the North-East — Ishanya, the water element — and sends weight to the South-West — Nairritya, earth. So underground water and the borewell belong North-East, North or East; the heavy overhead tank over the South-West or West.
Prayer room against a toilet, or a room tucked under the stairs

The prayer space and the toilet share a wall, or a room is tucked under the stairs. The tradition separates pure from impure by adjacency, not direction: a prayer space on a toilet wall is wrong anywhere in the home, and the same logic bars a store or toilet beneath a staircase. What is walked over should not be prayed beside, or kept in.
strings.concern: "by adjacency, not direction" — "adjacency" is the one properly technical word in the whole rule set, and the plain phrase ("by what shares a wall") is right there in the next clause.

strings.text: A road pointing straight at the plot

A road runs straight at the plot — Veedhi Shoola, the 'street spear'. Our reading treats a thrust from the South, South-West, South-East or North-West as harmful; from the North, North-East or East, benign. A stricter school calls every road-arrow harmful. The schools genuinely disagree, so this is shown but never counted in your score.
Heavy trees in the North-East or the centre

A heavy tree stands in the North-East or the centre — ground meant to stay light. The North-East should be the property's lightest, most open part; the centre is Brahma's square, which the Manasara text wants unweighted. A big tree sets permanent weight and shade on that ground. The same reasoning bars heavy storage from both places.
A mirror facing the bed, or a beam over a bed or desk

A mirror faces the bed, or a beam runs over it. Both rules are 20th-century additions to Vastu. We searched for a classical basis and found none — no text we examined rules on either. They are included because customers expect them, and labelled honestly as modern rather than ancient.
strings.concern: Directly contradicts the unlock screen's promise of "The classical source behind every rule we apply to your home". A paying reader finds, inside the thing they bought, the app saying there is no source.

strings.text: The home is long and narrow

The home is more than twice as long as it is wide. The mandala grid behind the reading is a square; the tradition calls a square, or a rectangle within about one-to-two, balanced — only then do the nine zones come out roughly equal. This plan stretches its zones thin one way, so the reading is less even.
Kitchen in the South-West

The kitchen's fire and bustle sit in the South-West, the corner meant to be stillest. The South-West is Nairritya — earth's element, the feet of the Purusha — kept heaviest and least disturbed; hence the master bedroom and heavy storage there. A kitchen, the busiest and hottest room, sets constant fire and movement there instead. Fire's own quarter is the South-East.
Kitchen in the centre

The kitchen stands on the centre, the square the texts ask to be left open. The centre is the Brahmasthan — Brahma's square, the element of space — which the Manasara text asks be left open and unbuilt. A kitchen is the opposite: heavily serviced, full of weight, heat and plumbing. Fire's own quarter is the South-East.
Master bedroom in the centre

The master bedroom stands on the centre, the square the texts ask to be left open. It is Brahma's square — traditionally the open courtyard — which the Manasara text asks stay open and unweighted. The master bedroom is the home's heaviest permanent room; its quarter is the South-West — Nairritya, earth, where weight should gather.
Bedroom in the South-East

A bedroom sits in the South-East, the fire corner. The South-East is Agneya — Agni's quarter, the element of fire — given to the kitchen and whatever generates heat. Rest is the opposite, so the tradition keeps sleeping out of the fire corner. A bedroom's own quarters are the West, Paschima, and the North-West, Vayavya.
Bedroom in the centre

A bedroom stands on the centre, the square the texts ask to be left open. The centre is the Brahmasthan, which the Manasara text wants open and unweighted. A bedroom — permanent, enclosed, furnished — is the opposite of open ground. Its own quarters are the West and the North-West.
Toilet in the centre

The toilet stands on the centre, the square the texts ask to be left open. The centre is Brahma's own square, reserved for the family's own deity — the demand comes from the Manasara text. A toilet — the one room held impure — thus stands on the plan's most reserved square. Its own quarter is the North-West, where air carries waste out.
Living room in the South-West

The living room — the home's busiest room — sits in the South-West, its most private corner. The South-West is Nairritya, the element of earth, kept heaviest and least disturbed — which is why the master bedroom and storage belong there. All-day coming and going works against that corner's purpose. A living room's own quarters are the North, East and North-East.
Living room in the centre

The living room stands on the centre, the square the texts ask to be left open. The centre is the Brahmasthan, which the Manasara text wants open and unweighted — in traditional homes it is the courtyard, not a room. Living here is not automatically wrong, but it is built ground on a square meant to stay clear. The heavier the furniture, the further from the rule.
Staircase in the North-East

The staircase — usually the home's heaviest structure — sits in the North-East, its lightest corner. The North-East is Ishanya, the head of the mandala grid, kept lightest and most open. A staircase is solid, permanent weight — it belongs opposite: the South, South-West and West.
Study in the South

The study sits in the South, the half of the home the tradition gives to rest. The South is Dakshina, Yama's quarter — given to rest, discipline and weight, not study. Study belongs where the desk can face East or North: the West — Paschima, Varuna's quarter of learning — or the North-West.
Study in the South-West

The study sits in the South-West, the corner given to rest and storage. The South-West is Nairritya, earth's element — the heaviest, most settled corner, given to sleeping and storage rather than work. A study belongs where the desk faces East or North: the West — Varuna's quarter of learning — or the North-West.
Store in the North-East

A store's stacked weight sits in the North-East, the corner meant to stay lightest. The North-East is Ishanya, the head of the mandala grid, kept lightest, cleanest and most open — and a store is weight that rarely moves. Storage belongs opposite: the South-West, West or South.
Garage in the North-East

The garage sits in the North-East, the corner meant to stay lightest and most open. A garage is heavy, closed and full of metal — everything Ishanya, the head of the mandala grid, should not hold. A vehicle belongs in Vayavya — the North-West, quarter of air and movement — or the South-East.
Garage in the South-West

The garage — the one thing that moves every day — sits in the South-West, the corner meant to stay still. The South-West is Nairritya, the anchor corner, kept most settled and least disturbed — and a garage sends something large in and out daily. A vehicle belongs in the North-West, the quarter of movement, or the South-East.
Balcony in the South-West

A balcony opens up the South-West, the corner meant to be most solid. A balcony takes weight out of a wall and lets the corner breathe — but the South-West is Nairritya, earth's element, kept heaviest and most closed. Balconies belong on the light side: the North, East and North-East.

strings.concern: "This fallback catches anything outside that list" is a sentence about the software, printed inside a paid report. It also calls the reader's room "this element".

screen: Report — the remedies (from the rule data)
whenSeen: Inside an opened problem, under "If it cannot move — remedies". Each line carries where it comes from, in brackets.

strings.text: Move or resize the element on the drawing so it leaves the wrong zone — free while the plan is still on paper. (From classical text)
strings.condition: Shown only to a reader who said they are building; stripped for buyers and residents
strings.concern: Two problems in one line. "the element" is engine vocabulary, and "free" is the same cost claim flagged twice above. It is also tagged "From classical text" while being an instruction about using this app's drawing tool.

strings.text: Keep the centre of the home open and unweighted — no heavy furniture, no storage, nothing built on it. The Manasara, a classical text, states this directly. It is the texts' one explicit instruction about the centre. (From classical text)
Keep the North-East itself light: low furniture, no heavy storage, nothing piled up, and as much daylight as the room allows. (Traditional practice)
Put the household's heaviest things against the South and West walls — the tallest wardrobe, the stored trunks. Weight then still gathers where the mandala grid places it. (Traditional practice)

Wherever the kitchen ends up, set the cooking platform against that room's South-East corner. Stand facing East to cook. The tradition fixes the hearth's own direction, not only the room's. (Traditional practice)
Keep water and fire apart inside the kitchen — sink and filter towards the North-East side, stove and gas towards the South-East side, not side by side. (Traditional practice)
Keep the toilet door shut and the room dry and ventilated. Keep its floor a step higher than the rooms around it. This is 20th-century practice — no classical verse prescribes it. (Modern practice)
A rock-salt bowl in the affected corner. 20th-century practice; no textual basis. (Modern practice)
strings.concern: Carries a product code in the data, so this line is a future shopfront sitting inside a report the customer already paid for. Nothing on screen discloses that.

strings.text: Sleep with your head to the South or the East, never to the North. Of all the direction rules, this is the one every school states alike. (Traditional practice)
Move the bed into the South-West corner of whichever room you sleep in. The sleeper then still rests on the heaviest part of that room. (Traditional practice)
Have the stair turn clockwise as you climb. Keep the space beneath it open — not closed in as a store or a toilet. (Traditional practice)
Sit facing East or North at the desk. Which way the person faces is fixed as firmly in the tradition as where the room sits. (Traditional practice)
Keep only light, seldom-used things in it — no heavy metal, no water drums, nothing stacked high — and keep the floor visible. (Traditional practice)
Keep the seating towards the North and East half of the room. Keep the heavy pieces against its South and West walls. (Traditional practice)
Park nose-out and keep the rest of that corner clear rather than using it for storage. 20th-century practice; no classical basis. (Modern practice)
Keep a South-West balcony roofed and screened rather than left open. Put the heavier planters and furniture on it. (Traditional practice)
Give the prayer space its own wall. A full-height cupboard, a shelf run or a service duct between it and the toilet is enough separation. (Traditional practice)
Give the entrance a raised threshold. Keep the approach to it clear, lit and unobstructed. The threshold is a real element in the texts, not a modern addition. (Traditional practice)
If there is another doorway on the North or East wall, make that the household's everyday door. Keep this one for service. (Traditional practice)
Leave the ground at the missing North-East corner open, clean and a little lower than the rest. Do not fill it in with a shed, a store or a parked vehicle. (Traditional practice)
A Tulsi plant near the North-East. Genuinely traditional (unlike money plant or lucky bamboo). (Traditional practice)
strings.concern: "Tulsi" is left unglossed — holy basil — on a paid screen, and the aside about money plant and lucky bamboo is the app arguing with rival practitioners in front of the customer.

strings.text: Follow the mandala grid with water. Overhead storage towards the South-West or West; underground water and the borewell towards the North-East, North or East. (Traditional practice)
Keep heavy trees off the North-East and off the centre. Put light planting, grass or open ground there instead. Keep the big canopy to the South or West. (Traditional practice)
Screen the side the road points at with a boundary wall or a line of planting. The schools disagree on whether the direction of the thrust matters at all. (Schools disagree)
Turn the mirror so it does not face the bed, or box the beam in behind a false ceiling. Modern practice; no classical basis found for either. (Modern practice)
Vastu Shanti / Vastu Puja — the genuine traditional pacification, prescribed in the Mayamatam, a classical treatise. (From classical text)

strings.text: A toilet in the East
A defect
Tradition holds a toilet spoils the East, the sun's quarter.
Acceptable in one strip

strings.text: A kitchen in the North
Not ideal
The North belongs to Kubera, lord of wealth. Tradition reads it as water, unsuited to the kitchen's fire.
Not ideal, not a fault
Modern practice calls a northern kitchen less than best, not a fault to correct.
The main bedroom in the West

strings.text: Acceptable
Tradition accepts the West, the other settled, heavier quarter, instead of the South-West.
Advised against
The 16-zone school keeps the main bedroom out of the west-south-west, its quarter of study.
strings.concern: "west-south-west" is a direction the app never draws, never scores and never names anywhere else.

strings.text: A front door in the South-East
Acceptable in the right position
The 32 named door positions sort good from bad within the South-East. Exact position, not direction, decides.
The Manasara, a classical Vastu treatise, says a home should never face the South-East.
Which way to sleep with your head
Head to the South is best
Tradition ranks head-to-South first, East next, West neutral.
Avoid head to the North
The one point every school agrees on. We pass it on as tradition, claiming nothing about your health.
Which way the idols face
Against the West or South-West wall
Classically, idols stand against the West or South-West wall, so the worshipper faces East.
Against the East wall
Modern practice often stands them against the East wall, facing West.
Where a septic tank belongs
The sources contradict each other
The North, North-West and South-East are each insisted on by serious sources.
Too sharp to rule on
strings.concern: "Too sharp to rule on" does not mean anything in ordinary English. The body underneath explains it; the label above it does not.

strings.text: Choosing one would invent a tradition. We report it as not checked unless you say where yours is.
A road pointing straight at the plot
It depends which direction
A road from the North-East, North or East is harmless. From the South, South-West, South-East or North-West comes the thrust tradition warns of.
Always harmful
The strict school treats any such road as a wound, from any direction.
A corner that sticks out
A North-East extension is welcome
Tradition reads a North-East extension as a good sign, not a fault.
Every extension is a fault
The strict school treats anything that sticks out as a fault, the North-East included.
Where the prayer room belongs
Classical — the centre
The family deity holds the centre of the home, as the Manasara sets out.
Modern — the North-East
Near-universal modern practice places the prayer room in the North-East.
Your score follows the modern reading: North-East ideal, North and East acceptable. No position counts as a defect, the classical centre included. The other school's advice never becomes a fault.

screen: Report — the reason each kind of room wants its direction (from the rule data)
whenSeen: Inside an opened room row, under the verdict. Free for the entrance, kitchen and toilets; behind the price for everything else.

strings.text: The main entrance is judged on a finer scale than the nine zones. It is read on the 32 named door positions along the mandala grid's edge. It is the highest-weighted single element in the whole reading.
strings.concern: "the highest-weighted single element" — weighted is scoring vocabulary and "element" here means the front door. Both appear in the report's own prose too.

strings.text: The kitchen is the household's fire. It belongs in the fire quarter: the South-East, Agneya, Agni's own corner. The North-West is the accepted second choice. It is Vayu's quarter of air, and air feeds fire. The tradition keeps the kitchen out of the water corner and the heavy corner.

The head of the household should rest on the heaviest, most settled ground. That is the South-West — Nairritya, the corner of earth. It holds the feet of the Purusha, the figure laid over the plan. The South and West are accepted: the same heavier half of the home.
strings.condition: Master bedroom
strings.concern: This is the ONLY place in the whole product that hints at what Purusha means — "the figure laid over the plan" — and it is locked behind the paywall, while the term is used unglossed on free screens.

strings.text: Ordinary bedrooms sit best in the West, Varuna's quarter, or the North-West, Vayu's. Varuna rules water; Vayu rules air. Both quarters are settled enough for rest. The South-West is kept for the head of the household. The tradition keeps sleeping out of the fire corner.

A prayer room belongs in the North-East — Ishanya, Ishana's quarter, the home's lightest, most sensitive part. The North and East, also kept open, are accepted next — Kubera's and Indra's quarters, from either of which a person at prayer still faces the rising sun. No direction is ruled out. The classical texts place the shrine at the very centre. We have chosen not to follow that reading, but we will not call it a defect.

What leaves the house belongs in the quarter of movement. That is the North-West — Vayavya, Vayu's own corner — or the West. The tradition keeps the toilet off the North-East, its most sensitive square. It keeps it off the South-West too — the home's anchor.

The living room is where the household gathers and guests are received. It belongs on the lighter, more open half: the North, the East and the North-East. These are the quarters of Kubera, Indra and Ishana. It is kept out of the heavy, private corner.

A staircase is the heaviest permanent structure in most homes. It goes where the tradition wants weight: the South, the South-West and the West. It is kept off the North-East, which should stay light. The Manasara, a classical text, asks that the centre be left open.

The study is placed so the person at the desk faces East or North while working. That points to the West — Varuna's quarter, which the tradition links with learning — or the North-West. The two heavy southern corners are kept for rest and storage, not work.
Dining sits best in the West, Paschima, close to the kitchen's fire corner without standing in it. The North and East are accepted. Nothing is outright prohibited for a dining room.

A store is stacked weight that seldom moves. It belongs in the heavy half: the South-West, the West or the South. Only the North-East is ruled out — the tradition wants that corner lightest and clearest.
The North-West is Vayavya, Vayu's quarter of movement. The tradition links it with things that come and go — exactly what a guest room is for. The West is accepted. Nothing is outright prohibited.

A vehicle comes and goes, so the North-West, the quarter of movement, suits it. The South-East is the other accepted place. It is kept off the North-East, which must stay light, and the South-West, which must stay undisturbed. The garage is a modern room the classical texts never placed. The rule is reasoned from what those two corners are for.
A balcony is an opening in a wall. It belongs on the light half: the North, East and North-East. The tradition wants the South-West solid and closed. So it is the one place a balcony is ruled out.

The tradition discourages a basement altogether, rather than placing it in a direction. The modern schools that do permit one disagree about where. We do not score a basement at all rather than pick a side.
